3.	 Towards a world constitutional order
Klaus Bosselmann
1.	
INTRODUCTION
Behind the notion of ‘world constitutional order’ lies the search for values and 
norms that bind people across all nations and cultures. This search is not new 
and has involved many great thinkers, such as Immanuel Kant. In his essay 
‘Toward Perpetual Peace’, Kant expressed the vision that the ‘use of the right 
to earth’s surface which belongs to the human race in common’ would ‘finally 
bring the human race to a cosmopolitan constitution’.1
Over the last decade or so, numerous initiatives for a global constitution 
have emerged2 and many international lawyers have embraced the concept of 
global constitutionalism.3 These developments have been described as a new 
way of thinking or ‘mindset’4 in response to our globalized world. Back in 
1987, the Brundtland Report proclaimed: ‘From One Earth to One World’.5 
This vision may or may not come to pass, but people are increasingly affected

Towards a world constitutional order

by common experiences and challenges regardless of where they happen to 
live. Humanity’s common destiny makes Kant’s dream of a cosmopolitan 
constitution a real prospect, at least in the long run. We certainly need a code 
of common values, rights and responsibilities.
The contributors to this book share the ambition for a value-based constitu-
tional order and perhaps no one more so than its celebrant. J. Ronald Engel is 
a co-creator of the Earth Charter and has always supported the Earth Charter 
movement with reflective solidarity and critical thought. In particular, he 
reminds us that we ought to live by the Earth Charter, not just believe in it. 
The difference between believing in a just, sustainable world and living by its 
values is vast. It is the difference between good intentions and real action. How 
can the gap between intentions and actions be closed?
Engel’s oeuvre is all about closing this gap. His plea is for living by the 
standards that we have set ourselves for our relationships with each other and 
with Earth. If it is possible to capture this plea in a word, it is the term ‘cov-
enant’. In its widest sense, a covenant is a solemn promise to do or not to do 
a particular thing. Originally from religious sources, it refers to love, respect, 
trust and engagement. Covenants create a certain bond between people. In 
Engel’s words: ‘Covenants are the unconditional pledges of free and equal 
individuals to principles and purposes that will enable them to engage in rea-
soned discourse and dialogue and cooperate for the common good while also 
protecting their respective differences and culture.’6 This definition helps us to 
understand, for example, why marriage and life partnership are covenants, but 
also what constitutes a community, whether small (family) or large (commu-
nities and societies).
Any community has a covenantal basis of some form and degree. The same 
is true of society and the law guiding it.
In law, covenants may be express or implicit. Examples of express covenants 
are the two major international human rights conventions, both passed in 1966. 
The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International 
Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights are agreements that gave 
legal force to the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights. While there 
are no official accounts as to why the term ‘covenant’ was chosen, this term 
distinguishes itself from ‘treaty’ or ‘convention’ through its characteristic as 
a unilateral promise: signatory states are saying that they will respect human 
rights irrespective of whether other states will do the same.

The crisis in global ethics and the future of global governance

An element of covenantal agreement is implicit in any piece of legislation 
produced by politicians and law makers. Law can work only if it is trusted and 
respected by its proponents and recipients. In the short run, plain enforcement 
– even against the will of recipients – may suffice; but on the whole, laws and 
constitutions depend on preconditions that they rely on, but cannot themselves 
guarantee.7 The preconditions are typically unwritten, hidden or assumed, and 
hence cannot be clearly defined and enforced.
The secular, rationalized world of law may not be aware of its covenantal 
roots and preconditions, but no lawyer worth his or her salt would deny their 
existence. Mutual trust and respect, for example, must be assumed when 
lawyers do their job. Similarly, laws in general rest on certain assumptions 
– for example, a general acceptance of their validity, trustworthiness and 
enforceability. What happens, though, if these assumptions can no longer be 
made? What if people think that laws – or any covenantal bond, for that matter 
– are not for them and can be ignored? Such thinking would lead to the erosion 
of the rule of law and eventually to the unravelling of the social web.
In our time of great volatility, how can we be confident that our institutions 
of social interaction and cooperation will remain? In a world that can no 
longer be sure about its key institutional arrangements – democracy, rule of 
law, respectfulness and decency – the search for consistency and permanence 
becomes pivotal. What is it that we should look for now? It is here that cov-
enantal thinking is most helpful, as it seeks to disclose what sustains us as 
human beings. Rather than merely speculating about the future – ‘Anything 
is possible’; ‘Who knows?’; ‘Who cares?’ – covenantal thinking has faith and 
direction. It is a fundamental belief in humanity – a kind of confidence that 
human values matter, that they are real and that we all ought to live by them.
In this context, the search for a world constitutional order makes good sense. 
The search can help us to identify human values and define them with respect 
to (non-enforceable) ethical norms and (enforceable) legal norms. It may not 
be necessary to actually draft a document and give it a name. There are, after 
all, many constitutional-type documents around human rights and human 
responsibilities. What matters are the covenantal characteristics underpinning 
them. Can they be articulated in a document?
Engel has made the claim that the Earth Charter is a covenant.8 Against the 
backdrop of the Faustian Pact – arguably the Western world’s most poignant

expression of sacrificing morality and connectedness at the altar of knowl-
edge – he locates the Earth Charter’s underpinnings as a covenantal plea for 
responsibility, integrity and connectedness.9 This makes the Earth Charter 
an unconditional pledge, quite beyond its quality as a document of values 
and principles. Identifying with the Earth Charter requires more than mere 
endorsement: it is the solemn promise to other people (today and in the future) 
to actively live by the values and principles expressed there.
The following explores some of the Earth Charter’s covenantal qualities 
in the search for a (true) world constitutional order that we as humanity can 
identify with.
2.	
THE EARTH CHARTER AS A COVENANT
The Earth Charter aims to build democratic societies that are just, participa-
tory, sustainable and peaceful. To this end, it promotes respect for nature, 
universal human rights, social and economic justice and a culture of peace. 
None of these is deemed possible, however, without a shared commitment to 
Earth. As the Preamble puts it: ‘(I)t is imperative that we, the peoples of Earth, 
declare our responsibility to one another, to the greater community of life, and 
to future generations. . . The protection of Earth’s vitality, diversity and beauty 
is a sacred trust.’ The language used here reveals covenantal thinking.10
The Earth Charter sits at the interface between global ethics and interna-
tional law, between good intentions and politics, and somewhere at the leading 
edge of world constitutional order. It provides, therefore, an excellent measure 
for what we as members of global civil society have achieved and what has 
yet to be done.
An unbiased investigation of this nature must start with the observation that 
the Earth Charter has fallen behind its own expectations. Societies today are 
less just, less participatory, less sustainable and less peaceful than 20 years ago, 
when the Charter was drafted and adopted. This is not just the result of rampant 
neo-liberalism or states not listening. There are systemic reasons having to do 
with the dynamics of capitalism, the revival of nationalism and militarism and, 
underpinning it all, the unfettered instrumentalization of humans and nature.

This process is closely associated with the development of Western ‘civiliza-
tion’ – and not just in its ugly manifestations of colonialism, imperialism and 
capitalism. The Enlightenment is part and parcel of this process; not that any 
of its achievements such as individual freedom, human rights and democracy, 
is inherently flawed. Today, however, we have to concede that these are 
more ideals than experienced realities. The instrumentalization of people 
has never stopped and now seems to affect everyone outside the tent (of the 
rich). Likewise, the instrumentalization of nature seems unbroken, reaching 
ever-new heights of altering the natural conditions of life (‘Anthropocene’).
None of the above is the Earth Charter’s ‘fault’; but this does not mean 
that we should exempt it – and ourselves, for that matter – from criticism 
and self-reflection. For example, how can the Earth Charter movement stay 
unfazed by the complete failure of states to control global economic forces? 
We care, of course; but does this not also require a rethink of motives, contents 
and future direction? Engel has important things to say here.11 Crucially, the 
Earth Charter movement must see itself as an integral part of global civil 
society and act accordingly. This may involve closer cooperation with human 
rights movements (women, children, refugees, workers/unemployed/poor), 
indigenous movements, the rights of nature movement, peace movements and 
democracy movements (‘the 99 per cent’), in this way taking a more political, 
strategic approach. It may also involve drafting new documents – for example, 
up-to-date commentary on the Earth Charter text or joint declarations of global 
civil society. In a general sense, the Earth Charter has yet to prove its leading 
role for ongoing debates on improving the living conditions of people and the 
integrity of planetary systems.
This chapter assumes the desirability of a world constitutional order. The 
Earth Charter plays a central role here, as it provides a tool for measuring 
success and failures as mentioned, but can also be seen as a model constitution, 
as will be shown. Consequently, the proponents of the Earth Charter should 
perceive themselves as at the vanguard of a global movement aiming for 
a world constitutional order.
We will first discuss the current state of international law to look for signs of 
coherence and direction. If there is a sufficient degree of coherence, as visible 
in treaties, principles and concepts, then it may be possible to perceive inter-

then be of great importance, as it intentionally sets out existing legal principles 
and concepts, as well as new ethical values and principles.
3.	
THE ‘GREENING’ OF INTERNATIONAL LAW
The Earth Charter perceives Earth as an indivisible whole12 and derives any 
environmental responsibilities of governments, business and civil society 
from there.13 In this way, it takes an Earth-centred perspective. By contrast, 
international law takes a state-centred perspective. Any environmental respon-
sibilities derive from agreements negotiated by, and for, states. Accordingly, 
Earth does not feature as a whole, but rather as an assembly of environmental 
phenomena (eg, ‘climate change’, ‘biodiversity loss’, ‘desertification’, ‘fisher-
ies’). Furthermore, environmental problems are addressed only as challenges 
to human development. The approach of international law is therefore reduc-
tionist in two respects: it is fragmented and anthropocentric.14 The system of 
international environmental treaties is hampered by fragmentation, conflicting 
purposes and the lack of an overall objective.15
Despite these shortcomings, there are signs of greater consistency and 
coherence. According to Andrew Long, international environmental law has 
developed a certain level of coherence through incorporation of unifying prin-
ciples in nearly every major treaty.16 Kiss and Shelton also spoke of a certain 
harmonization of international environmental law, due to the horizontal expan-
sion of norms, achieved through their inclusion in different legal instruments.17
When a new environmental agreement is adopted, it typically builds upon 
a number of existing agreements by way of recalling or reaffirming them.

In this way, a network of international agreements is created. International 
environmental law is, in fact, a closely connected and deeply intertwined field 
of law.18 This structural cohesion could be considered a sign of the maturation 
of international environmental law as a purposive system. It also indicates that 
a unifying core has emerged among diverse legally binding and non-binding 
agreements.
A converging point for divergent objectives of environmental agreements 
has been the notion of environment protection for sustainable development. 
All treaties or soft law agreements – whether they are about combating deser-
tification, regulating hazardous wastes or controlling fisheries – aim to protect 
sections of the global environment from human impact. Although the notion 
of sustainable development has entered treaty texts since the late 1980s,19 it is 
typically referenced as a higher ideal that should be promoted by meeting the 
immediate object and purpose of each agreement. For example, the objective 
of the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is ‘to achieve…
stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level 
that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate 
system’20 – that is, the protection of the climate system. The notion of sustain-
able development appears in the text as an eventual goal.21
The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, are 
another step of international law and governance seeking greater coherence 
and an overall purpose. However, the 17 SDGs are not mutually linked to each 
other. They are not guided by a definition of ‘sustainable development’ and are 
not legally binding.22
As has been shown elsewhere, the conceptual core of sustainable develop-
ment is ecological sustainability, defined as the integrity of Earth’s ecological 
systems.23
The notion of ecological integrity has been used as a key concept in a wide 
range of international environmental agreements. The first treaty to include the 
notion was the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living 
Resources, adopted in 1980, which recognized in its preamble ‘the importance 
of safeguarding the environment and protecting the integrity of the ecosystem

tainable development that allows each generation to satisfy its needs without 
compromising the capability of future generations to meet theirs’.33 This 
description resembles the Brundtland Report, which provided for more than 
just a general definition of ‘sustainable development’. Fundamentally, devel-
opment can only ever be ‘sustainable’ if it respects the ‘integrity of the natural 
system’ as the basic condition for ‘the survival of life on Earth’.34
Finally, the 1992 Rio Declaration, which is arguably the most authoritative 
text in international environmental law, states in the preamble that the UN 
Conference on Environment and Development worked towards ‘international 
agreements which respect the interests of all and protect the integrity of the 
global environmental and developmental system’.35 Furthermore, one of its 
main principles obligates states to ‘cooperate in a spirit of global partnership 
to conserve, protect and restore the health and integrity of the Earth’s ecosys-
tem’.36 This was in the spirit of the Brundtland Report and the World Charter 
for Nature of 1982, which firmly established the integrity of ecosystems or 
species as a non-negotiable bottom line when achieving ‘optimum sustainable 
productivity’ of natural resources.37

environmental law.38 But even independently of any legal status under inter-

Towards a world constitutional order

be without dispute. Surely, no one would doubt the fundamental importance of 
keeping the Earth’s life-supporting systems intact.
In sum, the ‘greening’ of international law can be described as a process 
of ongoing commitments to preserving the integrity of Earth’s ecological 
systems. The fact that this commitment has not been acted upon by states is 
irrelevant for the question of its legal quality. Ecological integrity has grown 
into a fundamental goal or grundnorm of constitutional quality. International 
law at large has developed a degree of coherence that allows its characterisation 
as a form of global constitutionalism.39 Another form of global constitutional-
ism, which has complemented international law development over the last 25 
years, is the ‘greening’ of national constitutions, in the sense of incrementally 
acknowledging environmental rights and environmental duties.40 The dual 
development of national and international environmental constitutionalism41 
allows us to speak of a global trend towards a world constitutional order or 
global constitution – at least in a rudimentary form.
4.	
LEGITIMACY OF A GLOBAL CONSTITUTION
Considering the actual feasibility and practicalities of a global constitution 
reveals numerous issues to be resolved. In particular, problems of legitimacy 
are apparent. While the drafting of a global constitution as such is still idealis-
tic, the discourse on global constitutionalism has generated many ideas around 
a constitution-type global document. The Earth Charter is arguably the best 
example of a constitution-type document. Can we legitimately speak of the 
Earth Charter as a draft global constitution?
Some commentators have expressed concern that the growing interest in 
global constitutional law may undermine existing domestic constitutions.42 
Fears include that supranational law may circumvent the domestic constitu-
tional law-making structure – for example, in the way that international cus-
tomary law is argued to have a direct effect in US courts; or that it may change 
the dynamics of the domestic law-making process, as where the World Trade 
Organization Agreement requires national implementation of rules formulated 
on the international plane. It may also affect enforcement procedures, by

Ernest Young is therefore wary that domestic law has checks and balances 
that ensure its legitimacy; and those features are somewhat different from the 
checks and balances that legitimize international law. Therefore, aspects of 
international law can conflict with domestic law. Indeed, it is generally agreed 
that when using the concept of ‘constitutionalism’ in the international sphere, 
as opposed to the domestic sphere, one cannot simply transfer the features 
associated with domestic constitutionalism to an international platform; the 
factors that make domestic constitutionalism legitimate become irrelevant 
on an international scale. Thus, in order to resolve the problems claimed by 
Young, scholars such as Anne Peters, Thomas Cottier and Mattias Kumm44 
suggest a new ground of legitimacy for global constitutional law that could 
rectify the clash of international and domestic constitutional law.
The legitimacy of traditional international law is based on the will and 
consent of sovereign states. That is because, since the Treaty of Westphalia 
in 1648, international law has been largely framed around the rights and 
duties of individual sovereign states. Because it is a mostly horizontal system 
of inter-state agreements, state consensus is all that is needed to make an 
agreement valid. Such a method cannot work in a vertical system. In a vertical 
system, there is a hierarchy of community interests and values that sit above 
the individual interests of states. The purpose of a discourse on a global consti-
tution is to protect those higher community interests and values. To that end, 
state consensus cannot, or cannot alone, be a legitimating factor of a global 
constitution. Brun-Otto Bryde explains this point with reference to human 
rights, saying that protection of human rights in international law has meaning 
only if it is recognized as a system of obligations of states owed to an authority

The constitutional mechanisms of ius cogens and erga omnes have already 
come into play to replace state consensus. Ius cogens signifies a norm that is 
considered of such importance that states cannot disregard it – whether they 
are in a treaty regarding the norm or not. For example, many human rights 
are ius cogens; therefore, any violation of a human right is a crime by a state. 
Obligations erga omnes complement ius cogens by creating obligations on all 
states to protect against and punish crimes which violate ius cogens. Some say 
that since these two devices are generally recognized in international law, the 
constitutionalization of international law is already developing. These mech-
anisms signify a value system that places state interests subordinate to them. 
The two legitimize international law, providing specific rules for all states to 
abide by.

THE CRITICAL ROLE OF CIVIL SOCIETY
Notwithstanding the many considerations that may speak in favour or against 
a global constitution from a legal point of view, there have always been strong 
voices within civil society. In fact, the basic values of any constitutionalism 
have been shaped and promoted by civil society. A prime example of these 
efforts is the history of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights 
(UDHR).
The morals and values of human rights can be traced through the history 
of many religious beliefs and cultures. In Europe, the philosophers of the 
Enlightenment developed theories of natural law that paved the way for the 
modern idea of fundamental human rights. The English Bill of Rights (1689), 
the American Declaration of Independence (1776) and the French Declaration 
of the Rights of Man and of the Citizens (1789) reflected this idea and inspired 
constitutionalism of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
